summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the aggregate assessment rates healthcare access as the single red flag against nine positive rights.

Detention is the sharpest exposure. Reporting by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté finds that trans detainees, overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement, suffer the most in the prison system, that administration policy recognises only biological sex, and that a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. A person detained in Saint Barthélemy falls under this same French system.

The controller-general's opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals received since 2010 and finds that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with its recommendations stated to apply also to intersex and non-binary persons.

For assessment context, the aggregate rating for the territory is 7.7 out of 10, built from nine positive rights and one red flag. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists for Saint Barthélemy, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office shows no warnings, and no trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.
tangentialFactors:
The island has no LGBTQ venues and no visible scene; there are no Pride-specific events. Discretion is the local norm, same-sex couples attract no attention, and no hostility toward visitors is reported in the sources.

The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are trained for diverse guests. Crime levels are described as low and the culture as open and accepting, which shapes day-to-day expectations independently of the legal position.

Rated 7.7 out of 10 in the aggregate index, the territory sits close to France's own coverage on paper while diverging on care access, which is the only red flag recorded against nine positive rights. The absence of any government travel warning means external advisories give a visitor no signal either way.

The prison findings belong to the metropolitan French detention system rather than to any local practice, so a trans visitor's realistic exposure runs through a shared national apparatus whose documented failures on placement are not specific to this island.
localsOnly:
Residents change their legal gender marker through the ordinary French administrative procedure, which requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, and the resulting French identity documents are the ones in force locally.

Non-binary status has no legal counterpart in French law, so residents hold documents in the male or female binary only, and the 2021 controller-general's recommendations on intersex and non-binary persons are the principal official recognition of that gap.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, but the territory's small scale and the healthcare red flag in the aggregate rating mean residents face restricted access to that care locally.

Residents held in custody fall under the French prison system, where administration policy recognises only biological sex and trans women are commonly placed by birth sex, the pattern the controller-general identifies as the most severe source of suffering for trans detainees.

The anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity and the 2023 ban on conversion practices bind here in full, and residents have the same marriage rights as in France since 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
No government LGBT+ travel advice is issued for Saint Barthélemy and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office records no warnings, so no official source addresses trans visitors directly; no trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted either, and the practical picture rests on general reporting.

Whether the 2021 recommendations of France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté have been implemented in facilities reachable from this territory is unresolved in the sources; only the existence of about 40 referrals since 2010 and the finding of persistent violations are documented.

The sources do not establish which facility would hold a detained trans visitor on the island, under what administration it operates, or whether transfers to metropolitan facilities apply; that chain is not sourced here.

No data is provided on local policing practice, hate-crime incidence, or how a gender marker is checked at the border, so entry-stage screening risk is not sourced.

The composition of the aggregate rating, in particular what the nine positive rights cover beyond the named items, is not itemised in the inventory and remains unresolved.
